title: Tensor Parallelism in Megatron-LM: How Column and Row Parallelism Shard Massive Models Across GPUs with Minimal All-Reduce Overhead
summary: When model parameters exceed the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) of a single GPU, engineers cannot simply replicate the model; they must split individual weight matrices across multiple devices. However, naive distributed matrix multiplications trigger excessive cross-GPU communication that saturates PCIe and NVLink interconnects. Megatron-LM solves this through an elegant pairing of column-parallel and row-parallel linear layers across Multi-Head Attention and Multi-Layer Perceptrons. By computing attention projections and non-linear activations locally on each GPU without inter-device synchronization, the entire transformer layer requires exactly two All-Reduce communication operations. This enables linear scaling across multi-GPU servers with minimal communication latency.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The 8-Chef Gourmet Line vs. The Chaotic Kitchen Meeting
analogy:
Imagine a high-end restaurant kitchen where an elaborate 10-course tasting menu must be prepared in under 3 minutes per plate. The master recipe (a 70-billion-parameter model) is far too massive for one chef to assemble alone on their cutting board.

If the kitchen uses naive task-splitting, Chef 1 chops the first vegetable, then blows a whistle and halts all 7 other chefs to announce the measurement. Chef 2 sautés the onion, blows the whistle again, and passes the pan around the room. Because every single culinary step requires a full-room announcement and synchronization, 90% of the chefs' time is spent waiting on chatter rather than cooking, and the kitchen grinds to a halt.

Megatron-LM Tensor Parallelism splits the prep station with mathematical precision. The 8 chefs stand along an ultra-fast conveyor line (NVLink). During the sauce course (Multi-Head Attention), each chef is assigned specific flavor heads: Chef 1 prepares garlic-ginger, Chef 2 prepares lemongrass-chili, and so on. They cook their specific flavor components completely independently in their own pans without speaking a single word.

Only when their individual flavor reductions are finished do they pour their sauces into a single master stock pot in the middle of the table—performing a single, synchronized All-Reduce. Next, for the vegetable glaze (MLP), each chef independently glazes their assigned batch of mushrooms using their own stove heat without communicating. Only when plating the final dish do they gather once more to stack their plates together. Across the entire complex recipe, the chefs talk exactly twice, letting them cook at maximum speed without stepping on each other's toes.

sections.heading: 1. The Memory Wall: Why Billion-Parameter Models Demand Intra-Layer Sharding
sections.content:
Modern frontier models—ranging from 70 billion to hundreds of billions of parameters—far exceed the High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) capacity of any single accelerator. A 70B model requires 140 GB of VRAM just to store weights in FP16 precision, completely exceeding the 80 GB limit of an NVIDIA A100 or H100. During inference and training, additional gigabytes are consumed by Key-Value (KV) caches, activation memory, and optimizer states.

Distributed architectures offer several strategies to distribute workloads, but each has structural tradeoffs:
• Data Parallelism (DP) replicates full model weights across all GPUs while distributing batches of data. If a single copy of the model cannot fit onto one GPU, pure Data Parallelism is impossible.
• Pipeline Parallelism (PP) partitions consecutive transformer layers across sequential GPUs (e.g., Layers 1–10 on GPU 0, Layers 11–20 on GPU 1). While PP fits massive models, it introduces 'pipeline bubbles' (idle idle time while waiting for activations to propagate forward and backward) and adds high sequential latency during single-request decoding.

To achieve low-latency inference and high throughput, systems require Tensor Parallelism (TP): splitting the weight tensors of every individual transformer layer across multiple GPUs connected via ultra-fast intra-node interconnects (such as NVLink running at 900 GB/s to 3.2 TB/s). The challenge is doing this without drowning the interconnect in cross-GPU communication.

sections.heading: 2. Column-Parallel and Row-Parallel Math: The Megatron-LM Insight
sections.content:
A transformer layer consists of two core sub-blocks: Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and the Feed-Forward Network (MLP / FFN). In standard matrix multiplication, calculating $Y = XW$ requires multiplying an input activation matrix $X$ by weight matrix $W$. The foundational insight of the Megatron-LM architecture is pairing Column-Parallel Linear layers with Row-Parallel Linear layers to cancel out intermediate communications.

1. Sharding Multi-Head Attention:
• Column-Parallel Projections ($W_Q, W_K, W_V$): The projection matrices are sliced along their columns across $N$ GPUs: $W = [W_1 \mid W_2 \mid \dots \mid W_N]$. Each GPU $i$ receives the identical input activation $X$ and independently computes $Y_i = X W_i$. Because multi-head attention heads operate independently, each GPU computes attention queries, keys, and values for its partition of attention heads (e.g., 32 heads divided across 4 GPUs = 8 heads per GPU) with zero inter-GPU communication.
• Row-Parallel Output Projection ($W_O$): The attention output projection matrix is sliced along its rows: $W_O = [W_{O,1}; W_{O,2}; \dots; W_{O,N}]^T$. Each GPU multiplies its local attention output with its row slice $W_{O,i}$. The final mathematical output is the sum $\sum_i \text{Attention}_i W_{O,i}$.
• Single All-Reduce Sync: At this point, the GPUs execute a single All-Reduce (Sum) operation to aggregate partial vectors into the final attention output, which is then added to the residual path.

2. Sharding the MLP Block:
• The first linear layer ($W_{gate}$ and $W_{up}$) is partitioned using Column Parallelism. Each GPU independently computes $X W_{1,i}$.
• The Non-Linear Activation Trick: Non-linear activations like GeLU or SwiGLU ($ ext{SiLU}(X W_{gate,i}) \odot (X W_{up,i})$) are strictly element-wise operations! Because each column output maps directly to its corresponding activation elements, each GPU applies the non-linear function locally without exchanging any data across GPUs.
• The second linear layer ($W_{down}$) is partitioned using Row Parallelism. Each GPU multiplies its activated intermediate tensor by its row partition $W_{down,i}$.
• A second All-Reduce (Sum) synchronizes the outputs before the final residual addition.

Across the entire transformer layer, Megatron-LM requires exactly two All-Reduce communications in the forward pass.

sections.heading: 3. Hardware Interconnect Limits, GQA Constraints, and 3D Parallelism
sections.content:
While Tensor Parallelism dramatically reduces communication compared to naive sharding, its high communication frequency dictates strict deployment rules:

• The NVLink Boundary: Because an All-Reduce occurs twice per layer (e.g., 160 All-Reduce calls per forward pass in an 80-layer model), TP is strictly confined within a single server chassis over high-bandwidth NVLink or NVSwitch fabrics. Running TP across Ethernet or PCIe buses introduces substantial latency bottlenecks that degrade throughput.
• Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) Constraints: Modern architectures like Llama 3 use Grouped-Query Attention where multiple query heads share a single Key-Value head (e.g., 8 KV heads for 64 query heads). In Tensor Parallelism, the number of KV heads must be evenly divisible by the TP degree. If an 8-KV-head model is deployed with TP=16, GPUs would hold fractional KV heads, requiring duplicate KV heads or complex head padding that inflates memory.
• 3D Parallelism Composition: In large-scale clusters, engineering teams compose Tensor Parallelism with Pipeline Parallelism (PP) and Data Parallelism (ZeRO / FSDP) to train models like Llama 3 405B. Typically, TP is set to 8 (spanning all 8 GPUs inside one HGX node), Pipeline Parallelism spans across multiple rack nodes, and Data Parallelism replicates the 3D pipeline across the broader datacenter cluster.

takeaway: When large language models exceed single-GPU memory limits or require ultra-low decoding latency, Tensor Parallelism shards individual weight matrices within each transformer block across NVLink-connected GPUs. By pairing Column-Parallel projections with Row-Parallel projections, Megatron-LM computes multi-head attention and non-linear activations completely independently on each device. This architectural insight reduces inter-GPU communication to exactly two All-Reduce operations per transformer layer, turning multi-GPU inference into a nearly linear speedup without communication bottlenecks.
